title: Nationalities and Languages
objective: State nationality and language(s): I'm…, I speak…; ask Do you speak…? as a chunk.
intro_md: [L1: In this lesson you learn to say your nationality ('I'm Mexican.') and your languages ('I speak Spanish and English.'). You also learn the question 'Do you speak English?' — learn it as one fixed phrase; the grammar behind it comes later.]
notes: Nationality set is keyed to three of the L05 countries (Mexican/Brazilian/Chinese) so every nationality has its country already taught; remaining §4 nationalities are budgeted to later lessons per the band file's region-personalization [proposed]. 'Do you speak English?' is taught as an unanalyzed chunk per §4 item 21 (do-support is U2). TODO_audio: exercises 2, 7, 8 carry the spoken line as written transcript in the prompt; audio assets not yet produced.

new_vocabulary.example_sentence: Do you speak English? Yes, I do.

exercises.prompt: language · English · Spanish · Mexican · Brazilian · Chinese · I speak… · Do you speak English?
exercises.rationale: Establish form-meaning link with audio for the nationality/language set and both new frames before any production.

exercises.prompt: [audio] 'She's from Mexico. She's Mexican.' — [L1: Which word says her nationality?]
exercises.rationale: Country vs nationality forms differ by one weak syllable (/koʊ/ vs /kən/); hearing the difference must precede producing it.

options.label: Mexican
options.rationale: The -an adjective form that follows 'She's' directly, with no 'from'.

options.label: Mexico
options.rationale: The country — used with 'from'; catches learners treating the two forms as interchangeable.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Match the country to the nationality.]
exercises.rationale: The three pairs use three different suffixes (-an, -ian, -ese): the mapping is item-by-item memory, not a rule — this exercise makes that explicit early.

exercises.prompt: A: Where are you from?  B: I'm from Brazil. I'm ___.
exercises.rationale: Form selection after 'be': 'Brazil' catches the high-frequency error 'I'm Brazil'; 'Mexican' checks meaning is driving the choice, not just word shape.
es yes/no questions need no auxiliary (¿Hablas inglés?), so the predicted error is 'You speak English?' — ordering forces the chunk to start with 'Do'.

exercises.prompt: A: ___ you speak English?  B: Yes, I ___.
exercises.rationale: 'Are you speak English?' is the documented overgeneralization of L05's be-questions; 'Speak you English?' is direct verb-fronting transfer. The short answer 'Yes, I do.' rides along as part of the chunk.

exercises.prompt: [audio] 'Do you speak Chinese?' — 'No, I don't. I speak English.' — [L1: Which language does the speaker speak?]
exercises.rationale: Two-turn listening: the answer contradicts the question, so the learner must track who says what and process the negation, not keyword-match.

options.label: English
options.rationale: Heard after 'I speak' in the answer turn.

options.label: Chinese
options.rationale: Heard only in the question — catches keyword-matching across turns without processing 'No, I don't.'

exercises.prompt: [audio] 'Do you speak Spanish?' → [L1: Answer truthfully, then say what you speak.]
asr_focus: 'I speak' frame produced (not 'I'm speak' — be-overgeneralization check)
exercises.rationale: Personalized production of the frame; ASR flags 'I'm speak', the merge of this lesson's two frames and the most likely blend error.

exercises.prompt: [L1: A new classmate asks where you are from, your nationality, and your languages. Answer, then ask them back.]
exercises.rationale: Integrates L05 origin frames with L06 nationality/language frames; the ask-back requirement pushes production of 'Do you speak…?', not just comprehension. Counts toward guided-interaction minutes.
